# Open-Source AI Models Are Moving to the Big Cloud Platforms

> **In short:** Meta has put an open-weight coding model on Together AI, and Flo Health has built safer custom AI on Databricks — together showing that open-source AI is moving onto major cloud platforms where everyday apps and businesses can use it more easily.

You don't need to be a developer to notice something shifting under the hood of AI. The big names — Meta, Databricks, Together AI — are quietly moving "open" AI models onto big hosted cloud platforms. That sounds like a tech-industry headline, but the ripple effect reaches the apps on your phone and the tools your employer uses every week.

Here's what's actually new, in plain words, and why it matters to you.

## What just happened

Meta says its Muse Spark Open model — designed for "agentic coding," meaning AI that can take actions and write code on its own — is now live on Together AI's cloud. According to Meta's announcement, it can handle a 1-million-token context window. A **token** is a small chunk of text (roughly four letters), so a million tokens is around 700,000 words — close to a long novel — all read at once.

Separately, Databricks shared a story about Flo Health, a health-tracking app with 81 million monthly users. Flo used Databricks' AI tools to build custom open-source models tuned for safer, more accurate answers in its product.

Two announcements, one direction: open AI models are leaving the lab and landing on the cloud platforms most businesses already use.

## What "open-weight" actually means

When a model is **open-weight** (sometimes called open-source), the underlying "settings" — the numbers the AI learned from during training — are published so anyone can download and run them. Compare that to a **closed** model like ChatGPT's, where only the company can see those settings.

Open doesn't automatically mean free or safe, though. It means *transparent*: people outside the company can study it, test it, and build on top of it. That's why smaller companies like Flo can take a base model and tune it for their own needs, instead of paying a giant AI company for every query.

## Why moving to the cloud is the big part

A model sitting on a hard drive is just a file. To be useful, it needs serious computers to run. Hosting platforms like Together AI and Databricks handle that "inference" — the moment the AI actually reads your question and produces an answer.

So when Meta puts Muse Spark Open on Together AI, a small startup in any country can plug it into their product without buying a warehouse full of servers. When Flo Health builds on Databricks, the company doesn't have to invent its own safety system from scratch — it gets the platform's tools along with the model.

## What this means for you

- **If you use everyday apps:** You're probably already using open models without realizing it. Health, finance, and travel apps increasingly run on open models hosted in the cloud, which is why responses feel faster and more personalized than they did two years ago.
- **If you work at a small business or as a freelancer:** Open models on big clouds mean custom AI tools are getting cheaper. A shop owner or solo consultant can now build a chatbot trained on their own FAQs without writing a single line of code, paying only for what they use.
- **If you care about safety and privacy:** The Flo Health story is worth watching. Health data is sensitive, and the company chose open models partly because they could audit them and add safety layers. As you hear more about "AI safety," ask whether the products you use can show their work.
- **If you're just curious about AI:** You don't need to use these tools directly to feel their effect. They shape the apps behind your banking, your streaming, and your doctor's office — quietly, in the background.
- **If you already use AI tools at work:** Pay attention to the platforms, not just the brand names. Knowing whether your company's AI runs on an open model in a hosted cloud helps you ask sharper questions about cost, privacy, and what happens if the vendor changes.

## Wrap-up

Two announcements, one underlying shift: open-source AI is settling onto the major cloud platforms, where real apps and real businesses can plug into it. You won't see a flashy consumer launch — but the apps you use every day are getting smarter, cheaper, and more customizable as a result. A simple next step: the next time an app gives you a surprisingly helpful answer, check the company's website or blog to see whether it runs on an open model in the cloud — that one small habit will tell you where AI is heading next.
